blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Quartiles, deciles and percentiles are values that divide sorted data into 4, 10 and 100 equal-sized parts. The pth percentile is the value below which a proportion p of the data lie. The median is the 50th percentile, which is also the 2nd quartile (Q2).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The median splits sorted data into two halves. Split into four and you get quartiles: Q1 (25th percentile), Q2 (the median) and Q3 (75th percentile). Deciles and percentiles are the same idea at finer resolution.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation: quartiles of raw data
blocks.html:
Several rules exist for placing a quartile between two observations, and software differs; R alone offers nine (Hyndman & Fan, 1996, via the R documentation). This book uses R’s default (type 7): the pth quantile sits at position 1 + (n − 1)p in the sorted data, interpolating between neighbours.

  1. Five children, sorted 9, 10, 11, 12, 13. Q1 position = 1 + 4 × 0.25 = 2 → Q1 = 10 kg. Q3 position = 1 + 4 × 0.75 = 4 → Q3 = 12 kg.
  2. Today’s 30 children, sorted (recall §1.4.1). Q1 position = 1 + 29 × 0.25 = 8.25: the 8th value is 10.5 and the 9th is 10.8, so Q1 = 10.5 + 0.25 × (10.8 − 10.5) = 10.575 kg.
  3. Q3 position = 1 + 29 × 0.75 = 22.75: the 22nd value is 12.9 and the 23rd is 13.1, so Q3 = 12.9 + 0.75 × 0.2 = 13.05 kg.

SPSS’s default rule (R type 6, position (n + 1)p) gives 10.45 and 13.175 kg for the same data. State the rule you used when you report quartiles from small samples.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation: quartiles from grouped data
blocks.html:
Replace N/2 in the grouped-median formula (recall §2.3) with the target position: Qk = L + [(kN/4 − cf) ÷ f] × h. Today’s 30 children (cumulative frequencies 5, 17, 26, 30):

  1. Q1: N/4 = 7.5 → class 10 to <12 (cf below = 5, f = 12). Q1 = 10 + [(7.5 − 5) ÷ 12] × 2 = 10.42 kg.
  2. Q3: 3N/4 = 22.5 → class 12 to <14 (cf below = 17, f = 9). Q3 = 12 + [(22.5 − 17) ÷ 9] × 2 = 13.22 kg.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A child whose weight sits at the 10th percentile of a growth chart weighs more than 10% of children of the same age and sex in the reference population, and less than 90%. The WHO Child Growth Standards are built by modelling the reference distribution at each age (the Box-Cox power exponential method) and are presented as both percentile curves and z-score curves (WHO Multicentre Growth Reference Study Group, 2006). A z-score counts standard deviations from the reference median; it is defined in §5.7.2.2.1 and applied to growth standards in §5.7.2.2.3.

points.html: Q1 = 25th percentile, Q2 = median = 50th percentile, Q3 = 75th percentile. Deciles D1…D9; percentiles P1…P99.
Like the median, these are positional measures: robust to outliers and valid for ordinal as well as skewed quantitative data.
Raw data: state the quartile rule. Grouped data: Qk = L + [(kN/4 − cf) ÷ f] × h, and any percentile Pp = L + [(pN/100 − cf) ÷ f] × h.
